long: A Bitcoin or Ethereum private key is just an integer chosen between 1 and n-1, where n is the order of the secp256k1 group, about 1.158 x 10^77, slightly below 2^256. Seed words, public keys, addresses and signatures are all math built on top of that one number. The whole security model assumes the number was picked truly at random from that huge range, far too large for any computer to guess. The series explains this math one fact per day.
tech: #Crypto Math #1: A Bitcoin or Ethereum private key is an integer from 1 to n-1, where n (the secp256k1 group order) is about 1.158 x 10^77, just under 2^256. All security rests on it being truly random. Daily series on the math behind it.
simple: #Crypto Math #1: Your coins aren't guarded by a vault. They're guarded by a number. A private key is one pick out of about 10^77 possibilities, far too many for any computer to guess. One fact a day on the math that guards your coins.
variant: #Crypto Math #1: Not a password, not a file: your crypto is a random number below about 1.158 x 10^77. Seed words, addresses, signatures are all math built on top of it. Let's open the box, one post a day.

card.title: Your private key is just a number
card.sub: One random integer from 1 to n-1. Seed words, addresses and signatures build on it.

long: Bitcoin and Ethereum use the same elliptic curve, secp256k1, a Koblitz curve defined in the SEC 2 standard. It is not one of the NIST curves like P-256 that most software relied on. Bitcoin chose it and Ethereum later reused it. Before Bitcoin became popular the curve was almost never used, so its wide adoption today comes almost entirely from crypto.
tech: #Crypto Math #2: secp256k1 is a Koblitz curve from the SEC 2 standard, not one of the popular NIST curves such as P-256. Bitcoin picked it and Ethereum followed. It was almost never used before Bitcoin.
simple: #Crypto Math #2: Bitcoin and Ethereum both use the same elliptic curve, called secp256k1. It was almost never used before Bitcoin: most software relied on the NIST curves instead.

card.title: One curve for Bitcoin and Ethereum
card.sub: secp256k1 is a Koblitz curve from SEC 2, almost never used before Bitcoin.

long: secp256k1 has a very short equation: y^2 = x^3 + 7, so a = 0 and b = 7. All arithmetic is done modulo the prime p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 977 (hex 0xFFFF...FFFEFFFFFC2F), a 78-digit number, so coordinates are whole numbers that wrap around p. The missing a*x term and the special form of p make fast implementations possible.
tech: #Crypto Math #3: secp256k1: y^2 = x^3 + 7 over the prime field p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 977 (0xFFFF...FFFEFFFFFC2F). No 'a*x' term, b = 7. That special shape enables fast implementations.
simple: #Crypto Math #3: The curve behind Bitcoin is a strikingly short formula: y^2 = x^3 + 7. All the math happens on whole numbers that wrap around a huge prime, 78 digits long.

card.title: A curve written in one short line
card.sub: All the math runs modulo a 78-digit prime, p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 977.

long: Unlike the NIST curves, whose constants cannot all be fully explained, secp256k1's parameters come from a predictable, non-random construction. That leaves less room for a deliberately planted weakness (a backdoor). The special structure also allows optimizations: a well-optimized implementation can be often more than 30% faster than on other curves.
tech:
#Crypto Math #4: Unlike the NIST curves, whose constants can't all be fully explained, secp256k1's parameters come from a predictable, non-random construction. That leaves less room for a planted weakness (a backdoor).

Its special structure also allows optimizations: a well-optimized implementation is often more than 30% faster than on other curves.
simple:
#Crypto Math #4: Why trust secp256k1? Its constants were chosen in a predictable way. That leaves less room for a hidden backdoor than curves whose constants can't be fully explained.

A side bonus: its simple structure lets software do the math faster. Well-optimized code can be more than 30% quicker than on other common curves.

card.title: Why trust the constants of secp256k1
card.sub: They follow a predictable construction, leaving less room for a hidden backdoor.

long: A public key is P = d*G: the private key d times the fixed generator point G, using elliptic curve scalar multiplication. Computing P from d is fast. Going back, recovering d from P, is the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP), believed infeasible for classical computers. Every wallet's security rests on that one-way property.
tech:
#Crypto Math #5: Public key P = d*G: scalar multiplication of the fixed generator point G by the private key d. Computing P from d is fast.

Going back, recovering d from P, is the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP), believed infeasible for classical computers. Every wallet's security rests on that one-way property.
simple:
#Crypto Math #5: Your public key is your private key multiplied by a fixed point on the curve. Going forward takes a split second. Going backward, from public key to private key, is believed infeasible.

That one-way street is the whole basis of crypto wallets: you can show your public key to everyone, and nobody can work out the secret behind it.

card.title: Easy one way, infeasible the other
card.sub: Public key = private key times a fixed point. Reversing it is the ECDLP.

long: A secp256k1 public key can be serialized in two ways. Uncompressed: prefix 0x04, then x and y, 65 bytes. Compressed: prefix 0x02 or 0x03 (the parity of y), then x only, 33 bytes. Since y^2 = x^3 + 7 gives two possible y for each x, one hint bit is enough to recompute y. Bitcoin Core defines SIZE = 65 and COMPRESSED_SIZE = 33 in pubkey.h.
tech:
#Crypto Math #6: Uncompressed pubkey: 0x04 || x || y = 65 bytes. Compressed: 0x02/0x03 (parity of y) || x = 33 bytes.

Since y^2 = x^3 + 7 gives two possible y for each x, one hint bit is enough to recompute y. Bitcoin Core defines SIZE = 65 and COMPRESSED_SIZE = 33 in pubkey.h.
simple:
#Crypto Math #6: A Bitcoin public key can be written in 65 bytes or just 33. The short form keeps x plus one hint for y, since y can be recomputed from the curve formula.

For each x on the curve, there are only two possible y values, one even and one odd. The first byte simply says which one, saving 32 bytes per key.

card.title: Same public key, 65 or 33 bytes
card.sub: The compressed form keeps x plus one hint bit; y is recomputed from the curve.

long: A 256-bit key does not give 256 bits of security. Generic attacks on the discrete log such as Pollard's rho need about sqrt(n) steps, i.e. about 2^128 group operations for secp256k1. So the curve targets a 128-bit security level, the target BIP340 also states. 2^128 is still far beyond any classical computer.
tech:
#Crypto Math #7: A 256-bit key doesn't give 256 bits of security. Generic attacks on the discrete log, like Pollard's rho, need ≈sqrt(n) steps: ≈2^128 group operations for secp256k1.

So the curve targets a 128-bit security level, the target BIP340 also states. 2^128 is still far beyond any classical computer.
simple:
#Crypto Math #7: A 256-bit key doesn't give 256 bits of security. The best attacks need about the square root of the work, so you get 128 bits. Still far beyond any classical computer.

2^128 is a number with 39 digits. Even if every computer on Earth tried for billions of years, they wouldn't come close to finding one key.

card.title: A 256-bit key, 128-bit security
card.sub: Pollard's rho needs about sqrt(n) steps. Still far beyond any classical computer.

long: A classic Bitcoin ECDSA signature is a pair of integers (r, s) encoded in DER. Its length varies. BIP62 notes that with the low-S rule and strict DER, S is at most 32 bytes and R at most 33, so a signature is at most 72 bytes and about 71.494 bytes on average.
tech:
#Crypto Math #8: A classic Bitcoin ECDSA signature is a pair of integers (r, s), DER-encoded, so its length varies.

BIP62: with the low-S rule and strict DER, S is at most 32 bytes and R at most 33, so a signature is at most 72 bytes and ≈71.494 bytes on average. Schnorr later fixed it at 64.
simple:
#Crypto Math #8: A classic Bitcoin signature is two numbers, r and s, wrapped in a format called DER. Its size varies a little: at most 72 bytes, about 71.5 on average.

The variation comes from how the format writes numbers: small values take fewer bytes. Taproot's newer Schnorr signatures are always exactly 64 bytes.

card.title: What an ECDSA signature weighs
card.sub: Two integers, r and s, encoded in DER. About 71.494 bytes on average.

long: ECDSA signs with s = k^-1 (z + r*d) mod n, where k is a secret per-signature nonce, z the message hash and d the private key. If the same k is used twice, both signatures share the same r. Anyone can then compute k = (z1 - z2)/(s1 - s2) and d = (s1*k - z1)/r. So a reused nonce leaks the private key through simple algebra, no hacking needed.
tech:
#Crypto Math #9: ECDSA: s = k^-1 (z + r*d) mod n, with k a secret per-signature nonce, z the message hash, d the private key. Two signatures with the same k share the same r.

Then anyone can compute k = (z1 - z2)/(s1 - s2) and d = (s1*k - z1)/r. A reused nonce is a leaked private key, through simple algebra.
simple:
#Crypto Math #9: Every ECDSA signature needs a fresh secret random number. Use the same one twice and anyone can compute your private key from just two signatures. No hacking, only algebra.

The reuse is even visible: both signatures share the same first value. Attackers scan the blockchain for exactly that pattern, then solve two equations.

card.title: Reuse a nonce, lose your key
card.sub: Two ECDSA signatures with the same k reveal the private key through simple algebra.

long: At the Chaos Communication Congress in 2010, the group fail0verflow showed that Sony's ECDSA code for the PS3 did not use a different random nonce for each signature. With two signatures using the same k, they could compute Sony's private signing key with the nonce-reuse algebra. A real-world example of how one randomness mistake breaks ECDSA.
tech:
#Crypto Math #10: PS3, Chaos Communication Congress 2010: fail0verflow showed Sony's ECDSA code did not use a different random nonce for each signature.

With two signatures sharing the same k, they computed Sony's private signing key with the nonce-reuse algebra. A real-world case of one randomness mistake breaking ECDSA.
simple:
#Crypto Math #10: In 2010, the hacker group fail0verflow showed that Sony signed PS3 software with the same "random" number every time. That one mistake exposed Sony's private signing key.

With that key, anyone could sign software as if they were Sony. The math of the signature was fine; the implementation broke it.

card.title: How Sony leaked its PS3 signing key
card.sub: fail0verflow showed Sony reused the same nonce. Two signatures were enough.

long: In August 2013 (alert of Aug 11), a flaw in Android's Java SecureRandom meant it could produce colliding values. Android Bitcoin wallet apps therefore produced ECDSA signatures with repeated r values, i.e. reused nonces. Attackers solved the private keys from those signatures and took the funds.
tech:
#Crypto Math #11: Aug 11, 2013 alert: a flaw in Android's Java SecureRandom meant it could produce colliding values. Android Bitcoin wallets therefore emitted ECDSA signatures with repeated r values, i.e. reused nonces.

Attackers solved the private keys from those signatures and took the funds.
simple:
#Crypto Math #11: August 2013: Android's random number generator had a flaw. Bitcoin wallet apps reused "random" values in signatures, thieves computed the private keys and took the coins.

The wallets relied on Android's default random generator, which was badly seeded, and the fix required apps to seed it properly.

card.title: When Android's randomness failed wallets
card.sub: A SecureRandom flaw repeated ECDSA nonces. Attackers solved the keys and took funds.

long: RFC 6979 removes the dependence on good randomness when signing: the ECDSA nonce k is derived deterministically from the private key and the message hash with HMAC-DRBG. The same message always gives the same k, and different messages give different k, so the nonce cannot repeat by bad luck or a broken RNG. libsecp256k1 supports this derandomized ECDSA.
tech:
#Crypto Math #12: RFC 6979 removes the need for good randomness when signing: the ECDSA nonce k is derived deterministically from the private key and message hash with HMAC-DRBG.

Same message, same k; different message, different k. The nonce can't repeat by bad luck or a broken RNG. libsecp256k1 supports this derandomized ECDSA.
simple:
#Crypto Math #12: The cure for bad random numbers in signatures: don't use them. Modern wallets compute the secret number from your key and the message, so it's unique per message and never left to chance.

Sign the same message twice, you get the same number, which is harmless. Sign two different messages, you always get two different numbers.

card.title: Signing without trusting the RNG
card.sub: The nonce comes from the key and message hash, so it cannot repeat by bad luck.

long: ECDSA is malleable: if (r, s) is valid, (r, n - s) is valid too, so anyone can change a signature without the key, which changed txids of non-SegWit transactions. BIP146's LOW_S rule requires s to be at most n/2 (0x7FFF...5D576E7357A4501DDFE92F46681B20A0). Bitcoin Core enforces it as relay policy, closing this third-party way to alter transactions.
tech:
#Crypto Math #13: ECDSA malleability: if (r, s) is valid, so is (r, n - s), so anyone can change a signature without the key, which changed txids of non-SegWit txs.

BIP146 LOW_S requires s <= n/2 (0x7FFF...5D576E7357A4501DDFE92F46681B20A0). Bitcoin Core enforces it as relay policy, closing this third-party way to alter txs.
simple:
#Crypto Math #13: Odd ECDSA quirk: every signature has a twin. Flip one value and it's still valid. Bitcoin nodes now only relay the "low" version, so outsiders can't tweak a signature.

Before that rule, anyone could flip a pending transaction's signature, which changed its ID without stealing anything, and confused software tracking payments.

card.title: Every ECDSA signature has a twin
card.sub: If (r, s) is valid, so is (r, n - s). Bitcoin relays only the low-S version.

long: Until 2015, Bitcoin relied on OpenSSL to parse signatures, and OpenSSL accepted various non-DER encodings. When OpenSSL 1.0.0p and 1.0.1k stopped accepting some of them, some nodes rejected the chain. BIP66 (strict DER, from Jan 2015) then made Bitcoin define its exact signature encoding rules itself. Lesson: consensus code cannot depend on a general library's quirks.
tech:
#Crypto Math #14: Until 2015, Bitcoin relied on OpenSSL to parse signatures, and OpenSSL accepted various non-DER encodings. When OpenSSL 1.0.0p and 1.0.1k stopped accepting some, some nodes rejected the chain.

BIP66 (strict DER, from Jan 2015) made Bitcoin define its exact encoding rules itself. Consensus can't depend on a library's quirks.
simple:
#Crypto Math #14: In 2015, an OpenSSL update changed which signatures it accepted, and some Bitcoin nodes rejected the chain. Lesson: consensus code can't rely on a general library's quirks.

A library update is normally harmless. In Bitcoin, if nodes disagree on one signature, they disagree on the whole chain. So Bitcoin wrote its own strict rules.

card.title: An OpenSSL update split Bitcoin nodes
card.sub: BIP66 then made Bitcoin define its own strict DER signature rules in 2015.

long: Bitcoin developers built libsecp256k1, a library dedicated to Bitcoin's curve. Bitcoin Core 0.12.0 (Feb 2016) switched ECDSA signature validation from OpenSSL to it. The release announcement says validation became up to 7x faster on 64-bit and that raw reindexing and block validation took less than half the time it did before.
tech:
#Crypto Math #15: Bitcoin developers built libsecp256k1, a library dedicated to Bitcoin's curve. Bitcoin Core 0.12.0 (Feb 2016) moved ECDSA validation from OpenSSL to it.

The release notes: validation up to 7x faster on 64-bit, and raw reindexing and block validation took less than half the time they did before.
simple:
#Crypto Math #15: Bitcoin developers wrote their own math library for its curve. When Bitcoin Core switched to it in 2016, checking signatures became up to 7 times faster.

Reindexing and validating blocks also took less than half the time. A library built for one curve and one job beat a general-purpose one, and cut reliance on OpenSSL for validation.

card.title: Bitcoin's own curve library pays off
card.sub: Bitcoin Core 0.12.0 moved to libsecp256k1: validation up to 7x faster on 64-bit.

long: Claus Schnorr's signature scheme (journal paper 1991) is simpler than ECDSA but was covered by US patent 4,995,082, which expired in February 2010. Bitcoin launched in January 2009, before that, and used ECDSA. Schnorr signatures only came to Bitcoin later, with Taproot and BIP340.
tech:
#Crypto Math #16: Claus Schnorr's signature scheme (journal paper 1991) is simpler than ECDSA but was covered by US patent 4,995,082, which expired in Feb 2010.

Bitcoin launched in Jan 2009, before that, and used ECDSA. Schnorr only came to Bitcoin later, with Taproot and BIP340.
simple:
#Crypto Math #16: Schnorr signatures are simpler than ECDSA, but they were patented. The patent only expired in February 2010, a year after Bitcoin launched with ECDSA.

Bitcoin launched with ECDSA, which was not covered by the Schnorr patent. It took until the Taproot upgrade, more than a decade later, for Schnorr signatures to finally arrive on Bitcoin.

card.title: The patent that kept Schnorr out
card.sub: US patent 4,995,082 expired in February 2010, after Bitcoin launched with ECDSA.

long: BIP340 Schnorr signatures have a fixed size of 64 bytes (R.x then s), while DER-encoded ECDSA signatures vary up to 72 bytes. Public keys are 32-byte x-only keys with an implicit even y, instead of 33-byte compressed keys. Less data on-chain means lower fees.
tech:
#Crypto Math #17: BIP340 Schnorr signatures have a fixed 64 bytes (R.x || s), while DER ECDSA signatures vary up to 72 bytes.

Public keys are 32-byte x-only keys with an implicit even y, instead of 33-byte compressed keys. Less data on-chain means lower fees, and a fixed size makes the signature's weight predictable.
simple:
#Crypto Math #17: Taproot's Schnorr signatures have a fixed size: always 64 bytes. Public keys shrink too, to 32 bytes. Less data on-chain means lower fees.

The old ECDSA signatures could take up to 72 bytes. Saving a few bytes per signature sounds small, but across millions of transactions it adds up.

card.title: Schnorr signatures have a fixed size
card.sub: Versus up to 72 bytes for ECDSA, with 32-byte x-only public keys. Lower fees.

long: BIP340 says Schnorr signatures are provably secure: strongly unforgeable under chosen message attack (SUF-CMA) in the random oracle model, assuming the elliptic curve discrete log problem (ECDLP) is hard. In contrast, the best known provable-security results for ECDSA rely on stronger assumptions.
tech:
#Crypto Math #18: BIP340: Schnorr signatures are provably secure, strongly unforgeable under chosen message attack (SUF-CMA) in the random oracle model, assuming the ECDLP is hard.

The best known provable-security results for ECDSA rely on stronger assumptions. Simpler math, cleaner proof.
simple:
#Crypto Math #18: Schnorr signatures come with a mathematical proof of security under standard assumptions. ECDSA's best known proofs need stronger assumptions.

In plain words: if the curve's basic hard problem holds, forging a Schnorr signature is provably as hard. For ECDSA, the guarantee rests on extra, less studied conditions.

card.title: Schnorr comes with a security proof
card.sub: Provably secure if ECDLP is hard. ECDSA's best proofs need stronger assumptions.

long: Schnorr verification is linear: s*G = R + e*P. If several signers add their nonces and their partial signatures, the result satisfies the same equation for the sum of their public keys. So keys and signatures can be added, and several people can jointly produce one signature valid for an aggregate key. This is the base of MuSig, MuSig2 and FROST.
tech:
#Crypto Math #19: Schnorr verification is linear: s*G = R + e*P. If several signers add their nonces and partial signatures, the result satisfies the same equation for the sum of their public keys.

So several people can jointly produce one signature valid for an aggregate key. It's the base of MuSig, MuSig2 and FROST.
simple:
#Crypto Math #19: Schnorr has a superpower called linearity: keys and signatures can be added. Several people can jointly make one signature valid for the sum of their keys.

This is what makes shared wallets look like normal ones. Each person signs their part, the parts are added up, and the result is one ordinary signature.

card.title: Keys and signatures that add up
card.sub: Schnorr is linear, so several signers can make one signature for a summed key.

long: BIP327 MuSig2 lets n signers create one aggregate public key and one ordinary 64-byte Schnorr signature. Per BIP327, MuSig2 Taproot outputs are indistinguishable for a blockchain observer from regular single-signer Taproot outputs, so a 3-of-3 wallet looks like a normal wallet and outsiders cannot tell that several people signed.
tech:
#Crypto Math #20: BIP327 MuSig2: n signers create one aggregate public key and one ordinary 64-byte Schnorr signature.

Per BIP327, MuSig2 Taproot outputs are indistinguishable for an observer from regular single-signer Taproot outputs, so a 3-of-3 wallet looks like a normal wallet. Smaller and more private.
simple:
#Crypto Math #20: With MuSig2, a 3-of-3 wallet looks exactly like a normal single-key wallet on the blockchain. Outsiders can't tell that several people signed.

It's also cheaper: one key and one signature on-chain instead of three of each. Privacy and lower fees from the same trick.

card.title: A multisig that looks like one key
card.sub: MuSig2 Taproot outputs are indistinguishable from regular single-signer ones.

long: MuSig2 needs only two communication rounds, while earlier schemes like MuSig1 needed three. The first round, exchanging nonces, can be done in advance, before the message or the exact set of signers is known. Once the session is fixed, signers send partial signatures with no further interaction.
tech:
#Crypto Math #21: MuSig2 is a two-round multisig, while MuSig1 needed three. Round 1, the nonce exchange, can be done in advance, before the message or exact set of signers is known.

Once the session is fixed, signers send partial signatures with no further interaction. Fewer rounds of communication make it easier to use between separate signers.
simple:
#Crypto Math #21: MuSig2 needs only two rounds of messages between signers, and the first round can be done before you even know what you'll sign.

So when it's time to sign, each person just sends their part once. That matters when signers are on different devices or not online at the same time.

card.title: MuSig2 cuts signing to two rounds
card.sub: The nonce round can happen in advance, before the message is even known.

long: BIP340 chose the (R, s) signature form, verified with s*G = R + e*P, because it puts no elliptic curve operations inside the hash. That allows batch verification: a node can check many signatures together faster than one by one. Per BIP340, standardized ECDSA cannot be batch-verified more efficiently without extra witness data.
tech:
#Crypto Math #22: BIP340 picked the (R, s) form, verified with s*G = R + e*P, because it puts no curve operations inside the hash. That enables batch verification: checking many signatures together faster than one by one.

Per BIP340, standard ECDSA can't be batch-verified more efficiently without extra witness data.
simple:
#Crypto Math #22: Schnorr signatures can be checked in batches: a node can verify many signatures together, faster than checking each one separately.

A block holds thousands of signatures. The design also allows checking many signatures as one batch, faster than one by one.

card.title: Checking signatures in bulk
card.sub: Schnorr allows batch verification: many signatures checked faster than one by one.

long: BIP340 tagged hashes compute SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || x), with a tag like 'BIP0340/challenge'. The 64-byte prefix is exactly one SHA-256 block, so implementations can precompute it as a modified initial state. The point is domain separation: a hash made for one purpose cannot be reinterpreted as a hash for another.
tech:
#Crypto Math #23: BIP340 tagged hashes: SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || x), with a tag like "BIP0340/challenge". The 64-byte prefix fills exactly one SHA-256 block, so it can be precomputed as a modified initial state.

The point: domain separation. A hash made for one purpose can't be reinterpreted as a hash for another.
simple:
#Crypto Math #23: Taproot hashes carry a label, like "BIP0340/challenge", so a hash made for one purpose can never be mistaken for a hash made for another.

Without labels, a clever attacker might reuse a hash from one context in another. The label costs almost nothing and removes that whole class of tricks.

card.title: Hashes that carry a label
card.sub: Tags like 'BIP0340/challenge' stop a hash being reused for another purpose.

long: In Taproot (BIP341), the output key is Q = P + hash(P || m)*G, where P is an internal key and m the Merkle root of a tree of alternative spending scripts. A key-path spend is a plain signature and reveals nothing about the scripts, so backup rules stay hidden. A script-path spend reveals only the branch actually used.
tech:
#Crypto Math #24: Taproot (BIP341) output key: Q = P + hash(P || m)*G, where P is an internal key and m the Merkle root of a tree of alternative spending scripts.

A key-path spend is a plain signature and reveals nothing about the scripts, so backup rules stay hidden. A script-path spend reveals only the branch actually used.
simple:
#Crypto Math #24: A Taproot address can hide a whole set of backup spending rules inside one public key. Spend the normal way, and nobody learns those rules existed.

The rules are mixed into the key with a hash. If you ever need a backup rule, you reveal just that one, and the others stay secret forever.

card.title: Backup rules hidden in one key
card.sub: A key-path Taproot spend is a plain signature that reveals nothing about the scripts.

long: Taproot stores its spending scripts in a Merkle tree. To spend with one script, you reveal it plus a control block of 33 + 32m bytes, where m, the Merkle path length, is between 0 and 128. BIP341 caps it at 128 because a script with less than a 1 in 2^128 chance of being used is beyond the security bound anyway. Only the used branch is revealed.
tech:
#Crypto Math #25: Taproot stores spending scripts in a Merkle tree. To spend with one, you reveal it plus a control block of 33 + 32m bytes, Merkle path length m from 0 to 128.

BIP341 caps m at 128 because a script with less than a 1 in 2^128 chance of being used is beyond the security bound anyway. Only the used branch is revealed.
simple:
#Crypto Math #25: Taproot stores spending scripts in a tree. To use one, you reveal only that branch and a short proof, not every possible condition.

The proof grows slowly: each extra level of the tree adds just 32 bytes. So a wallet can have many backup rules and still spend cheaply.

card.title: Reveal only the branch you use
card.sub: Taproot scripts sit in a Merkle tree, with the path length capped at 128.

long: Taproot (BIP340, 341 and 342) activated at block 709,632 on November 14, 2021. It added Schnorr signatures and SegWit version 1 outputs to Bitcoin, alongside the existing ECDSA.
tech:
#Crypto Math #26: Taproot (BIP340/341/342) activated at block 709,632 on Nov 14, 2021.

It added Schnorr signatures and SegWit version 1 outputs (bc1p addresses) to Bitcoin, alongside the existing ECDSA, which still works for older output types. Two signature schemes now coexist on the same chain, each tied to its output type.
simple:
#Crypto Math #26: Schnorr signatures went live on Bitcoin with the Taproot upgrade in November 2021, at block 709,632.

They didn't replace the old ECDSA signatures: both coexist. Older addresses keep using ECDSA, while new Taproot addresses (starting with bc1p) use Schnorr.

card.title: Taproot goes live on Bitcoin
card.sub: Activated on November 14, 2021, adding Schnorr signatures and SegWit v1 outputs.

long: A Bitcoin block's hash is SHA256(SHA256(header)) of an 80-byte header: version (4 bytes), previous block hash (32), Merkle root (32), time (4), nBits target (4) and nonce (4). Changing any bit gives a completely different hash. Miners vary the nonce and other fields until the hash meets the target.
tech:
#Crypto Math #27: Block hash = SHA256(SHA256(header)) of an 80-byte header: version (4 bytes), prev block hash (32), Merkle root (32), time (4), nBits target (4), nonce (4).

Changing any bit gives a completely different hash. Miners vary the nonce and other fields until the hash meets the target.
simple:
#Crypto Math #27: A Bitcoin block's ID is the fingerprint of a tiny 80-byte header, run through SHA-256 twice. Change one bit of the block and the ID changes completely.

The header includes the previous block's ID, which chains all blocks together. Change an old block and every ID after it breaks.

card.title: A block ID is a double SHA-256
card.sub: Hash a tiny header twice. Change one bit and the hash changes completely.

long: Bitcoin's genesis block hash is 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, starting with ten zeros. Proof of work is valid when the block hash, read as a 256-bit number, is below the target encoded in nBits. Leading zeros are what a number below a target looks like, so mining is a hunt for such hashes.
tech:
#Crypto Math #28: Bitcoin's genesis block hash: 000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f, starting with ten zeros.

Valid proof of work = the hash, read as a 256-bit number, is below the target encoded in nBits. Leading zeros are what a number below a target looks like.
simple:
#Crypto Math #28: Bitcoin's very first block has an ID starting with ten zeros. Mining is a hunt for a hash that starts with enough zeros, i.e. a number below a target.

Since hashes are unpredictable, the only way to find one is to try again and again. The more zeros required, the more tries it takes.

card.title: The genesis block's string of zeros
card.sub: Leading zeros are what a hash below the target looks like. Mining hunts for them.

long: BIP141 notes that by the end of 2015, about 2^84 hashes had been computed in Bitcoin mining since its creation, so 2^80 work 'is not infeasible anymore'. That is why SegWit's P2WSH commits to a 32-byte SHA-256 of the script rather than a 20-byte hash: the total mining work changed which hash sizes count as safe.
tech:
#Crypto Math #29: BIP141 notes that by the end of 2015, ≈2^84 hashes had been computed in Bitcoin mining since its creation, so 2^80 work "is not infeasible anymore".

That's why SegWit's P2WSH commits to a 32-byte SHA-256 of the script instead of a 20-byte hash: total mining work changed which hash sizes count as safe.
simple:
#Crypto Math #29: By the end of 2015, Bitcoin miners had computed about 2^84 hashes in total. A number that big changed which hash sizes count as safe.

If the world can do 2^84 hashes, an attack needing "only" 2^80 is within reach. So SegWit chose longer, 256-bit hashes for scripts shared between several people.

card.title: Mining work changed safe hash sizes
card.sub: By the end of 2015, that many hashes made 2^80 work no longer infeasible.

long: By the birthday paradox, finding a collision in an n-bit hash takes about 2^(n/2) tries, so about 2^80 for a 160-bit hash, not 2^160. A malicious co-signer could grind such a collision on a P2SH multisig. BIP141's P2WSH uses a 256-bit SHA-256 instead, making its scriptPubKey 34 bytes versus 23 bytes for P2SH.
tech:
#Crypto Math #30: Birthday paradox: a collision in an n-bit hash takes ≈2^(n/2) tries, so ≈2^80 for a 160-bit hash, not 2^160. A malicious co-signer could grind such a collision on a P2SH multisig.

P2WSH (BIP141) uses a 256-bit SHA-256 instead, making its scriptPubKey 34 bytes vs 23 for P2SH.
simple:
#Crypto Math #30: Birthday paradox: finding two inputs with the same 160-bit hash takes about 2^80 tries, not 2^160. That's why SegWit multisig scripts use 256-bit hashes.

Same idea as the classic puzzle: in a room of just 23 people, two likely share a birthday. Collisions come much sooner than intuition says.

card.title: Birthday math for hash collisions
card.sub: A 160-bit hash collides in about 2^80 tries, so P2WSH uses 256-bit SHA-256.

long: P2PKH and P2WPKH outputs do not contain the public key, only HASH160 of it: RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(pubkey)), a 20-byte fingerprint made with two different hash functions in a row. Bitcoin Core's CHash160 class applies SHA-256 first, then RIPEMD-160.
tech:
#Crypto Math #31: P2PKH and P2WPKH outputs don't contain the public key, only HASH160 = RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(pubkey)): a 20-byte fingerprint made with two different hash functions in a row.

Bitcoin Core's CHash160 class applies SHA-256 first, then RIPEMD-160. The full key only appears when the coin is spent.
simple:
#Crypto Math #31: A classic Bitcoin address doesn't contain your public key, only a fingerprint of it, hashed by two different functions in a row.

That makes the address shorter: 20 bytes instead of 33. And your actual public key stays off the blockchain until the day you spend those coins.

card.title: An address is a fingerprint of your key
card.sub: HASH160 runs SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160, giving a 20-byte fingerprint.

long: Legacy Bitcoin addresses use Base58, whose alphabet is 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz (from Bitcoin Core's base58.cpp). It is the digits and letters minus 0, O, I and l, the characters easiest to confuse when reading or copying by hand, which leaves 58 symbols.
tech:
#Crypto Math #32: Base58 alphabet (Bitcoin Core base58.cpp): 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz.

58 symbols: the digits and letters minus 0, O, I and l, the characters easiest to confuse when reading or copying by hand. The format trades a little compactness for fewer human errors.
simple:
#Crypto Math #32: Old-style Bitcoin addresses never contain 0, O, I or l. They were left out because they're too easy to confuse when reading or copying by hand.

Is it a zero or the letter O? A capital I or a small l? Removing them leaves 58 characters, hence the name of the format: Base58.

card.title: Base58 drops look-alike characters
card.sub: No 0, O, I or l: they are too easy to confuse when copying by hand.

long: Base58Check appends a 4-byte checksum, the first 4 bytes of SHA256(SHA256(payload)). A typo almost always fails it, but it cannot locate the error. BIP173 lists among base58's drawbacks that this double SHA256 checksum is slow and has no error-detection guarantees.
tech:
#Crypto Math #33: Base58Check appends a 4-byte checksum: the first 4 bytes of SHA256(SHA256(payload)). A typo almost always fails it, but it can't locate the error.

BIP173 lists among base58's drawbacks that this double SHA-256 checksum is slow and has no error-detection guarantees, one reason for Bech32.
simple:
#Crypto Math #33: Legacy addresses end with a 4-byte checksum, a hash of the rest. A typo almost always fails the check, but it can't tell you where the mistake is.

And "almost always" isn't a guarantee. That's one reason newer bc1 addresses switched to a code designed specifically to catch typing errors.

card.title: A checksum that can't find the typo
card.sub: Base58Check adds 4 bytes of double SHA-256. It flags errors but cannot locate them.

long: Bech32 addresses (bc1, BIP173) use a BCH code as checksum. It guarantees detection of any error affecting at most 4 characters, and has less than a 1 in 10^9 chance of failing to detect larger errors. Bech32 strings are at most 90 characters. The guarantee is mathematical, not just a probability, for small typos.
tech:
#Crypto Math #34: Bech32 (bc1, BIP173) uses a BCH code as checksum: guaranteed detection of any error affecting at most 4 characters, and less than a 1 in 10^9 chance of missing larger errors.

Bech32 strings are at most 90 characters. For small typos, the guarantee is mathematical, not just a probability.
simple:
#Crypto Math #34: bc1 addresses (Bech32) use an error-detecting code: any typo touching up to 4 characters is always caught. Guaranteed, not just likely.

For bigger mistakes, the chance of slipping through is under one in a billion. It's the same family of math used to protect data on CDs and in satellites.

card.title: Typo detection with a guarantee
card.sub: Bech32 always catches errors touching up to 4 characters, by math, not luck.

long: BIP173 says decoders MUST NOT accept mixed-case Bech32 strings. A single case avoids base58's mixed-case problems (hard to write down, type on mobile keyboards or read aloud), and uppercase can be used in QR codes, whose alphanumeric mode is more compact. Lowercase is preferred for display.
tech:
#Crypto Math #35: BIP173: decoders MUST NOT accept mixed-case Bech32 strings. One case avoids base58's mixed-case pain: hard to write down, type on mobile keyboards or read aloud.

Uppercase can be used in QR codes, whose alphanumeric mode is more compact. Lowercase is preferred for display.
simple:
#Crypto Math #35: Why are bc1 addresses all lowercase? A single case is easier to read aloud, type on a phone and fit into QR codes. Mixed case is rejected.

Try dictating "capital A, small b, capital C" over the phone. A single case avoids all that, and in all-caps, QR codes can store the address more compactly.

card.title: Why bc1 addresses use one case
card.sub: A single case is easier to read aloud, type on a phone and pack into QR codes.

long: BIP350 describes an unexpected Bech32 weakness: whenever the final character is 'p', inserting or deleting any number of 'q' characters immediately before it does not invalidate the checksum. Existing SegWit v0 addresses were not affected because they are restricted to two specific lengths, but future uses could be.
tech:
#Crypto Math #36: BIP350 describes an unexpected Bech32 weakness: whenever the final character is "p", inserting or deleting any number of "q" characters just before it doesn't invalidate the checksum.

Existing SegWit v0 addresses weren't affected, since they're limited to two specific lengths, but future address types could be.
simple:
#Crypto Math #36: Bech32 had a surprise flaw: if an address ends in "p", you can add or remove "q" letters just before it and the checksum still passes.

Old bc1q addresses were safe because they must have one of two exact lengths. New address types needed a fix before they could use the format.

card.title: Bech32's surprise flaw with 'p' and 'q'
card.sub: Insert or delete 'q' before a final 'p' and the checksum still passes.

long: The fix is Bech32m (BIP350): same design, but the constant XORed into the checksum at the end changes from 1 to 0x2bc830a3. SegWit v0 outputs (P2WPKH, P2WSH, bc1q addresses) keep Bech32, while witness versions 1 through 16, including Taproot (bc1p), use Bech32m.
tech:
#Crypto Math #37: The fix is Bech32m (BIP350): same design, but the constant XORed into the checksum at the end changes from 1 to 0x2bc830a3.

SegWit v0 outputs (P2WPKH, P2WSH, bc1q) keep Bech32, while witness versions 1 to 16, including Taproot (bc1p), use Bech32m. Decoders pick the variant from the witness version.
simple:
#Crypto Math #37: The fix is called Bech32m: same design, one constant changed. Taproot addresses (bc1p...) use it; older bc1q addresses keep Bech32.

One number in the formula changed, and the weakness was gone. Wallets just need to know which version to apply depending on the address type.

card.title: Bech32m: one constant changed
card.sub: Taproot bc1p addresses use Bech32m, while SegWit v0 bc1q addresses keep Bech32.

long: An Ethereum address is the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key, where the public key is the 64-byte x || y without the 0x04 prefix. In geth's code: Keccak256(pubBytes[1:])[12:]. 20 bytes is 40 hex characters, which is why addresses are 0x plus 40 hex digits.
tech:
#Crypto Math #38: Ethereum address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(public key), where the public key is the 64-byte x || y without the 0x04 prefix. In geth: Keccak256(pubBytes[1:])[12:].

20 bytes = 40 hex characters, hence 0x plus 40 hex digits. The raw format has no checksum; EIP-55 added one later via capitalization.
simple:
#Crypto Math #38: An Ethereum address is the last 20 bytes of a hash of your public key. That's why every address is 40 hex characters after the 0x.

Unlike Bitcoin, there's only one way to make it, and no built-in checksum in the raw format. That's why a capitalization trick was added later.

card.title: Where Ethereum addresses come from
card.sub: The tail of the Keccak-256 hash of the public key: 40 hex characters.

long: Ethereum's hash is often called SHA-3 but is the original Keccak-256, not the FIPS 202 SHA3-256 standard. Both use the same permutation but different padding, so they give different outputs for the same input. geth builds its hasher with NewLegacyKeccak256.
tech:
#Crypto Math #39: Ethereum's hash is often called SHA-3 but is the original Keccak-256, not FIPS 202 SHA3-256. Both use the same permutation but different padding, so they give different outputs for the same input.

geth builds its hasher with NewLegacyKeccak256. Using the "official" SHA3 by mistake gives wrong results.
simple:
#Crypto Math #39: Ethereum's hash is often called "SHA-3", but it isn't exactly. It's the original Keccak, which gives different outputs from the official SHA3-256.

Ethereum adopted Keccak before the standard was finalized with a small change. So a developer using the official SHA-3 library gets different hashes.

card.title: Ethereum's 'SHA-3' isn't SHA3-256
card.sub: It's the original Keccak-256: same permutation, different padding and output.

long: EIP-55 adds a checksum to Ethereum addresses through capitalization: hex letter i is uppercased if bit 4*i of Keccak-256 of the lowercase hex address is 1. On average this gives 15 check bits per address, and EIP-55 states that a mistyped random address passes the check with a probability of 0.0247%. That's why addresses show random capital letters.
tech:
#Crypto Math #40: EIP-55 checksums Ethereum addresses through capitalization: hex letter i is uppercased if bit 4*i of Keccak-256 of the lowercase hex address is 1.

On average this gives 15 check bits per address, and EIP-55 states a mistyped random address passes with a probability of 0.0247%. Hence the random capitals.
simple:
#Crypto Math #40: Ever noticed random capital letters in Ethereum addresses? They're a checksum. A mistyped address has only about a 0.02% chance of passing it.

The pattern of capitals comes from a hash of the address itself. Change a character, and the expected pattern no longer matches, so your wallet warns you.

card.title: The checksum hidden in capital letters
card.sub: EIP-55 encodes about 15 check bits per address through letter case.

long: Ethereum transactions carry a signature (v, r, s) but no 'from' field. Nodes recover the sender's public key from the ECDSA signature (ecrecover) and derive the address from it. v encodes the parity of y of the curve point whose x is r, which tells the recovery which of the two possible points to use.
tech:
#Crypto Math #41: Ethereum txs carry a signature (v, r, s) but no "from" field. Nodes recover the sender's public key from the ECDSA signature (ecrecover) and derive the address from it.

v encodes the parity of y of the curve point whose x is r, which tells the recovery which of the two possible points to use.
simple:
#Crypto Math #41: Ethereum transactions don't say who sent them. Nodes compute the sender's public key from the signature itself, then derive the address.

That saves space in every transaction. And it can't be faked: only the true owner of the key could have produced a signature that recovers to that address.

card.title: Transactions with no sender field
card.sub: Nodes recover the sender's public key from the signature, then derive the address.

long: EIP-155, from block 2,675,000, adds replay protection: transactions are signed over (nonce, gasprice, startgas, to, value, data, chainid, 0, 0), and v is set to {0,1} + CHAIN_ID*2 + 35. Mainnet has CHAIN_ID = 1. Since the chain ID is inside the signature, a transaction signed for one network cannot be replayed on another.
tech:
#Crypto Math #42: EIP-155 (from block 2,675,000) adds replay protection: txs are signed over (nonce, gasprice, startgas, to, value, data, chainid, 0, 0), and v = {0,1} + CHAIN_ID*2 + 35. Mainnet CHAIN_ID = 1.

The chain ID is inside the signature, so a tx signed for one network can't be replayed on another.
simple:
#Crypto Math #42: Since EIP-155, an Ethereum signature includes the chain's ID, so a transaction signed for one network can't be replayed on another.

Before it, a payment made on one Ethereum-style chain could be copied and broadcast on another chain with the same accounts. Mainnet's ID is 1.

card.title: One signature, one network
card.sub: EIP-155 puts the chain ID inside the signature to block cross-chain replays.

long: EIP-712 defines signing of typed structured data instead of raw bytes: the signed payload is \x19\x01 || domainSeparator || hashStruct(message). Wallets can show readable fields to the user, and the domain separator binds the signature to one app and contract, so it cannot be reused elsewhere. Users should still read the fields before signing.
tech:
#Crypto Math #43: EIP-712 signs typed structured data instead of raw bytes: the payload is \x19\x01 || domainSeparator || hashStruct(message).

Wallets can show readable fields, and the domain separator binds the signature to one app and contract, so it can't be reused elsewhere. Users should still read the fields before signing.
simple:
#Crypto Math #43: When a dApp asks for a signature, EIP-712 lets your wallet show readable fields instead of a blob of hex. Read them before you sign.

The signature is also tied to one specific app and contract, so it can't be reused somewhere else. But it can still authorize something you didn't mean to.

card.title: Readable signatures with EIP-712
card.sub: Wallets show typed fields bound to one app and contract. Read them before signing.

long: BIP39: the checksum is the first ENT/32 bits of SHA256(entropy), appended to the entropy. For 12 words, 128 bits of entropy + 4 checksum bits = 132 bits = 12 words of 11 bits. Because 4 bits must match, only about 1 in 16 random 12-word combinations is a valid phrase.
tech:
#Crypto Math #44: BIP39: the checksum is the first ENT/32 bits of SHA256(entropy), appended to the entropy. For 12 words: 128 bits of entropy + 4 checksum bits = 132 bits = 12 words of 11 bits.

Because 4 bits must match, only ≈1 in 16 random 12-word combinations is a valid phrase.
simple:
#Crypto Math #44: A 12-word seed phrase holds 128 bits of randomness plus a 4-bit checksum. That's why 12 random words are rarely a valid phrase: only about 1 in 16 is.

The last word isn't free: part of it is computed from the others. That's why you can't just pick 12 words you like and call it a seed.

card.title: Most random 12-word phrases are invalid
card.sub: 128 bits of entropy plus a 4-bit checksum make 132 bits, 12 words of 11 bits.

long: For 24 words, BIP39 uses 256 bits of entropy plus an 8-bit checksum: 264 bits = 24 x 11. The last word holds 3 entropy bits and 8 checksum bits, so it is mostly checksum, and only 8 of the 2048 words can complete a given 23-word start.
tech:
#Crypto Math #45: For 24 words, BIP39 uses 256 bits of entropy + an 8-bit checksum: 264 bits = 24 x 11.

The last word holds 3 entropy bits and 8 checksum bits, so it's mostly checksum: only 8 of the 2048 words can complete a given 23-word start. A forgotten last word is trivially recoverable by trying those 8.
simple:
#Crypto Math #45: A 24-word seed holds 256 bits of randomness plus an 8-bit checksum. The 24th word is mostly checksum: it carries only 3 bits of randomness.

Out of 2048 possible words, only 8 can validly finish a given set of 23. If you forget only the last word, it's easy to recover.

card.title: The 24th word is mostly checksum
card.sub: It holds only 3 entropy bits next to 8 checksum bits.

long: BIP39 splits entropy plus checksum into 11-bit groups. Each group is a number from 0 to 2047, an index into a list of exactly 2048 words, because 2^11 = 2048. So 12 words encode 2048^12 = 2^132 possibilities.
tech:
#Crypto Math #46: BIP39 splits entropy + checksum into 11-bit groups. Each group is a number from 0 to 2047, an index into a list of exactly 2048 words, because 2^11 = 2048.

So 12 words encode 2048^12 = 2^132 possibilities, of which 4 bits are checksum: 128 bits of real entropy. The words are just a human-friendly encoding of one number.
simple:
#Crypto Math #46: The seed phrase word list has exactly 2048 words. Each word encodes 11 bits, because 2^11 = 2048.

Your seed is really one huge number, cut into 11-bit slices. Each slice picks a word from the list. The words are just an easier way to write that number down, and the order of the words matters.

card.title: Why the word list has 2048 words
card.sub: Each word is an 11-bit index, so 12 words encode 2^132 possibilities.

long: In the BIP39 English list of 2048 words, no two words share the same first 4 letters, so typing or writing 4 letters is enough to identify a word unambiguously. The list also avoids similar word pairs (like build/built) to limit memorization and transcription errors.
tech:
#Crypto Math #47: BIP39 English wordlist: 2048 words, and no two share the same first 4 letters, so typing or writing 4 letters identifies a word unambiguously.

The list also avoids similar word pairs (like build/built) to limit memorization and transcription errors. Useful for metal backups with limited space.
simple:
#Crypto Math #47: In the English seed word list, the first 4 letters of each word are unique. Write down just 4 letters and the word can still be recovered.

That's handy for metal backup plates with little room. The list also avoids look-alike pairs, like "build" and "built", to prevent copying mistakes.

card.title: Four letters are enough per word
card.sub: No two BIP39 English words share their first 4 letters, so each is unambiguous.

long: BIP39 itself lists, among its shortcomings, that the checksum is short: it only gives modest odds of catching random errors (1 in 256 errors will be missed, the 8-bit case of 24 words; with 12 words and 4 bits it's 1 in 16). It also cannot help correct errors or say which word is wrong.
tech:
#Crypto Math #48: BIP39 itself lists, among its shortcomings, that the checksum is short: with 8 bits (24 words), 1 in 256 random errors is missed; with 12 words (4 bits), 1 in 16.

It also can't help correct errors or say which word is wrong. A phrase that passes the checksum isn't proof it was copied correctly.
simple:
#Crypto Math #48: The seed checksum is short. BIP39's own text says it gives modest odds of catching random errors, and it can't tell you which word is wrong.

With 12 words, about 1 in 16 wrong phrases still passes the check. So a "valid" phrase isn't proof you wrote it correctly: check your backup carefully.

card.title: The seed checksum is admittedly short
card.sub: BIP39's own text says it misses some errors and can't say which word is wrong.

long: A BIP39 phrase is not used directly as the key. It goes through PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512: password = the mnemonic (UTF-8 NFKD), salt = 'mnemonic' + optional passphrase, 2048 iterations. The output is a 512-bit (64-byte) seed. The iterations make each guess slower.
tech:
#Crypto Math #49: A BIP39 phrase isn't used directly as the key. It goes through PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512: password = the mnemonic (UTF-8 NFKD), salt = "mnemonic" + optional passphrase, 2048 iterations.

The output is a 512-bit (64-byte) seed. The iterations make each guess slower.
simple:
#Crypto Math #49: Your seed phrase isn't used as-is. It goes through 2048 rounds of hashing to become a 512-bit master seed, which makes guessing slower.

For you, the delay is a fraction of a second. For an attacker testing billions of guesses, every round of hashing multiplies the cost.

card.title: Your phrase is hashed before use
card.sub: PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 turns it into a 512-bit seed, slowing each guess.

long: BIP39's optional passphrase (the '25th word') goes into the PBKDF2 salt. Every passphrase produces a valid seed and wallet, which BIP39 presents as plausible deniability. The flip side: a typo in the passphrase silently opens a different, empty wallet instead of giving an error.
tech:
#Crypto Math #50: BIP39's optional passphrase (the "25th word") goes into the PBKDF2 salt. Every passphrase produces a valid seed and wallet, which BIP39 presents as plausible deniability.

The flip side: a typo in the passphrase silently derives a different, empty wallet instead of giving an error.
simple:
#Crypto Math #50: A seed passphrase (the "25th word") opens a completely different wallet. Any passphrase is valid, so a wrong one shows an empty wallet, never an error.

That can protect you: under pressure, you can reveal a decoy wallet. But forget the exact passphrase, even one capital letter, and your real wallet is gone.

card.title: The 25th word opens another wallet
card.sub: Every passphrase is valid, so a typo shows an empty wallet instead of an error.

long: BIP32 turns one seed into a whole key tree. First step: I = HMAC-SHA512(key = 'Bitcoin seed', data = seed). The left 32 bytes are the master private key, the right 32 bytes the chain code, an extra 256 bits of entropy that extends the key. From this master key, billions of addresses can be derived.
tech:
#Crypto Math #51: BIP32 turns one seed into a whole key tree. First step: I = HMAC-SHA512(key = "Bitcoin seed", data = seed).

The left 32 bytes are the master private key, the right 32 bytes the chain code, an extra 256 bits of entropy that extends the key. From this master key, billions of addresses can be derived.
simple:
#Crypto Math #51: One seed can produce billions of addresses. Step one: hash the seed with the fixed phrase "Bitcoin seed" to get a master key.

From that master key, the wallet derives child keys, then grandchildren, like a family tree. That's why one backup restores every address you ever used.

card.title: One seed, billions of addresses
card.sub: BIP32 hashes the seed with 'Bitcoin seed' to get a master key and chain code.

long: In BIP32, each extended key has 2^31 normal children (indices 0 to 2^31-1) and 2^31 hardened children (2^31 to 2^32-1), about 4.3 billion in total. Hardened derivation uses the parent private key rather than the public key, which limits the damage if a key leaks.
tech:
#Crypto Math #52: BIP32: each extended key has 2^31 normal children (indices 0 to 2^31-1) and 2^31 hardened children (2^31 to 2^32-1), ≈4.3 billion in total.

Hardened derivation uses the parent private key rather than the public key, which limits the damage if a key leaks.
simple:
#Crypto Math #52: Each key in an HD wallet has about 4.3 billion possible children: half "normal", half "hardened". Hardened ones limit the damage if a key leaks.

Normal children can be computed from public information, which is handy for watch-only wallets. Hardened ones need the private key, which builds a firewall.

card.title: How many children an HD key has
card.sub: Half normal, half hardened. Hardened ones limit the damage if a key leaks.

long: BIP32 warns that knowing a parent extended public key (xpub) plus any non-hardened private key derived from it is equivalent to knowing the parent extended private key, and so every key below it. Sharing an xpub seems to reveal only balances, but one leaked child key exposes the whole branch. That's why account levels use hardened derivation.
tech:
#Crypto Math #53: BIP32 warning: a parent extended public key (xpub) plus any non-hardened child private key derived from it is equivalent to the parent extended private key, and so every key below it.

Sharing an xpub seems to reveal only balances, but one leaked child key exposes the whole branch. Hence hardened account levels.
simple:
#Crypto Math #53: Sharing your xpub only reveals balances, right? Unless one child private key also leaks. Then an attacker can rebuild every key under that xpub.

That's why wallets use hardened steps at the account level: a leak in one account can't spread to the others. Treat your xpub as sensitive.

card.title: Sharing an xpub is riskier than it seems
card.sub: With one leaked child private key, every key under that xpub can be rebuilt.

long: BIP44 defines the path m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. Purpose is 44, coin type 0 is Bitcoin, and ' marks hardened steps. A string like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 tells the wallet which branch of the key tree to use, so the same seed with the same path gives the same address in any compatible wallet.
tech:
#Crypto Math #54: BIP44 path: m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. Purpose is 44, coin type 0 is Bitcoin, and ' marks hardened steps.

A string like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 tells the wallet which branch of the key tree to use, so the same seed + same path gives the same address in any compatible wallet.
simple:
#Crypto Math #54: That string m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 in wallet settings is a path: it tells the wallet which branch of its key tree to use. The ' marks a hardened step.

If you restore your seed in a new wallet and see a zero balance, the path is often the culprit: the new wallet is simply looking in a different branch.

card.title: Reading a derivation path
card.sub: m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 tells the wallet which branch of its key tree to use.

long: SLIP-39 applies Shamir's secret sharing to seed backups: a seed is split into shares with a threshold, for example any 3 of 5. Shares use a 1024-word list (10 bits per word), and the last 3 words are an RS1024 checksum. With fewer shares than the threshold, nothing about the seed is learned.
tech:
#Crypto Math #55: SLIP-39 applies Shamir's secret sharing to seed backups: a seed is split into shares with a threshold, e.g. any 3 of 5.

Shares use a 1024-word list (10 bits per word), and the last 3 words are an RS1024 checksum. With fewer shares than the threshold, nothing about the seed is learned.
simple:
#Crypto Math #55: You can split a seed into shares, say any 3 of 5. With fewer than 3 shares, an attacker learns nothing about the seed. That's Shamir's secret sharing.

So you can store shares in different places. Lose one or two, you can still recover. A thief who finds one or two gets nothing useful.

card.title: Split a seed into shares
card.sub: With fewer shares than the threshold, nothing about the seed is learned.

long: BIP352 Silent Payments let a receiver publish one static address while each payment goes to a fresh output. The sender tweaks the output using ECDH (a*B = b*A) with the sum of its input keys; the receiver scans transactions for P = B + hash(b*A)*G. No on-chain notification is needed and payments are not linkable on-chain.
tech:
#Crypto Math #56: BIP352 Silent Payments: a receiver publishes one static address while each payment goes to a fresh output. The sender tweaks the output with ECDH (a*B = b*A) over the sum of its input keys.

The receiver scans for P = B + hash(b*A)*G. No on-chain notification is needed, and payments aren't linkable on-chain.
simple:
#Crypto Math #56: Silent Payments let you publish one static address, yet every payment lands at a fresh address that only you can find.

The sender and you share a secret computed from your keys, without ever talking. Outsiders just see unrelated payments, with nothing linking them to your public address.

card.title: One static address, fresh outputs
card.sub: Silent Payments use ECDH so only the receiver can find each payment.

long: A block's transactions are summarized in a Merkle root. When a level has an odd number of hashes, Bitcoin duplicates the last one, which is unusual. As a result, some different transaction lists give the same root (duplicate txids): CVE-2012-2459. Bitcoin Core's Merkle code warns about this and detects the mutation.
tech:
#Crypto Math #57: A block's txs are summarized in a Merkle root. When a level has an odd count, Bitcoin duplicates the last hash, which is unusual.

As a result, some different tx lists give the same root (duplicate txids): CVE-2012-2459. Bitcoin Core's Merkle code warns about this and detects the mutation.
simple:
#Crypto Math #57: A block's transactions are summed up in one hash, the Merkle root. With an odd count, Bitcoin copies the last hash, a quirk that once enabled a bug.

A tampered block with a duplicated transaction could have the same root as the real one, and trick nodes into rejecting it. Nodes now check for it.

card.title: A Merkle tree quirk that enabled a bug
card.sub: With an odd count, Bitcoin duplicates the last hash, so some lists share a root.

long: A Merkle proof needs only about log2(n) hashes. For a block of 4,096 transactions, 12 sibling hashes (12 x 32 = 384 bytes) link a txid to the Merkle root in the header, instead of downloading the whole block. This is the basis of SPV light wallets.
tech:
#Crypto Math #58: A Merkle proof needs only ≈log2(n) hashes. For a block of 4,096 txs, 12 sibling hashes (12 x 32 = 384 bytes) link a txid to the Merkle root in the header, instead of downloading the whole block.

This is the basis of SPV light wallets: they keep only 80-byte headers and ask for proofs.
simple:
#Crypto Math #58: To prove a payment is in a block of about 4,000 transactions, you need only about 12 hashes, not the whole block. That's how light wallets check payments.

Each hash climbs one level up the tree, until it reaches the root stored in the block header. A few hundred bytes instead of megabytes.

card.title: Proving a payment without the block
card.sub: A Merkle proof needs about log2(n) hashes. This is how SPV light wallets work.

long: Brain wallets derived the private key directly from a memorable phrase: private key = SHA256(passphrase). Attackers hashed huge lists of phrases and swept funds. Ryan Castellucci's DEF CON 23 talk (2015) and his Brainflayer tool showed how cheaply such keys can be cracked at scale. Humans are bad random generators.
tech:
#Crypto Math #59: Brain wallets derived the private key directly from a memorable phrase: private key = SHA256(passphrase). Attackers hashed huge lists of phrases and swept funds.

Ryan Castellucci's DEF CON 23 talk (2015) and his Brainflayer tool showed how cheaply such keys can be cracked at scale. Humans are bad random generators.
simple:
#Crypto Math #59: "Brain wallets" turned a memorable phrase into a private key. Attackers just hashed huge lists of phrases and swept the funds. Humans make bad random generators.

Song lyrics, quotes, clever puns: all were tried by bots in seconds. A phrase you can remember is a phrase someone else can guess.

card.title: Humans are bad at randomness
card.sub: Brain wallets hashed a memorable phrase into a key. Attackers hashed phrase lists.

long: Milk Sad, CVE-2023-39910: Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x 'bx seed' used the MT19937 Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with 32 bits of clock time, so only about 2^32 (4 billion) possible wallets, all enumerable. Attackers stole about 29.65 BTC, with the funds sent on July 12, 2023; per the disclosure, over $900K of crypto assets in total were moved.
tech:
#Crypto Math #60: Milk Sad, CVE-2023-39910: Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x "bx seed" used the MT19937 Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with 32 bits of clock time: only ≈2^32 possible wallets, all enumerable.

Attackers stole ≈29.65 BTC, sent on July 12, 2023; per the disclosure, over $900K of crypto in total was moved.
simple:
#Crypto Math #60: Milk Sad (2023): a command-line wallet tool built seed phrases from a 32-bit clock-based seed. Only about 4 billion possible wallets, all crackable. Over $900K was stolen.

4 billion sounds big, but a computer can try them all quickly. A real seed has 2^128 possibilities or more: a gap of 29 digits.

card.title: Milk Sad: wallets from a clock seed
card.sub: Only about 4 billion possible wallets, all enumerable. Over $900K was moved.

long: Randstorm: the JSBN library's SecureRandom(), used in BitcoinJS until March 2014, looked for window.crypto.random, which browsers didn't provide, and silently fell back to Math.random(), a weak random function. Browser wallets created around 2011-2015 may therefore have weak keys.
tech:
#Crypto Math #61: Randstorm: the JSBN library's SecureRandom(), used in BitcoinJS until March 2014, looked for window.crypto.random, which browsers didn't provide, and silently fell back to Math.random(), a weak random function.

Browser wallets created around 2011-2015 may therefore have weak keys.
simple:
#Crypto Math #61: Randstorm: browser wallets made around 2011-2015 may have weak keys, because an old JavaScript library quietly fell back to a weak random function.

The library looked for a secure random source that browsers didn't offer, and used a weak one without warning.

card.title: Randstorm and the silent fallback
card.sub: An old JavaScript library fell back to Math.random(), leaving weak browser keys.

long: In November 2022, the Trust Wallet browser extension generated seeds with effectively only 32 bits of entropy, so every possible seed could be enumerated and knowing an address was enough to rebuild its key. Ledger Donjon found it; the fix was committed on Nov 21, 2022 and the issue disclosed on Apr 22, 2023.
tech:
#Crypto Math #62: Trust Wallet browser extension, Nov 2022: seeds were generated with effectively only 32 bits of entropy, so every seed could be enumerated, and knowing an address was enough to rebuild its key.

Found by Ledger Donjon; fix committed Nov 21, 2022, disclosed Apr 22, 2023.
simple:
#Crypto Math #62: In 2022, a wallet browser extension generated seeds with only 32 bits of randomness. Knowing an address was enough to rebuild its key. Ledger's researchers caught it.

New weak seeds were stopped, but wallets already created stayed exposed until users moved funds; the full story came out months later. Same lesson as other cases: weak randomness turns strong math into nothing.

card.title: A wallet extension with tiny entropy
card.sub: Knowing an address was enough to rebuild its key. Ledger Donjon found the flaw.

long: Vanity addresses like 0x0000... are made by brute-forcing keys. On Sep 20, 2022, market maker Wintermute lost $160M from a vault whose admin was a Profanity vanity address. 1inch had just disclosed that keys from the Profanity generator could be brute-forced.
tech:
#Crypto Math #63: Vanity addresses like 0x0000... are made by brute-forcing keys. Sep 20, 2022: market maker Wintermute lost $160M from a vault whose admin was a Profanity vanity address.

1inch had just disclosed that keys from the Profanity generator could be brute-forced, because of how it seeded its search.
simple:
#Crypto Math #63: Vanity addresses look cool (0x0000...), but in 2022 a flawed generator, Profanity, made keys that could be brute-forced. Market maker Wintermute lost $160M.

A pretty address is made by generating many keys until one fits. If the generator starts from a weak random seed, attackers can redo the search.

card.title: When vanity addresses backfire
card.sub: Keys from the Profanity generator could be brute-forced, hitting Wintermute's vault.

long: On Feb 19, 2017, Monero found a CryptoNote bug: adding a small-order (torsion) point to an ed25519 key image let one output be spent up to 8 times, enough to create coins undetected. It was patched quietly first, and Monero's chain was never exploited. The fix checks that key images lie in the prime-order subgroup.
tech:
#Crypto Math #64: Feb 19, 2017: Monero found a CryptoNote bug: adding a small-order (torsion) point to an ed25519 key image let one output be spent up to 8 times, enough to create coins undetected.

It was patched quietly first; Monero's chain was never exploited. The fix checks that key images lie in the prime-order subgroup.
simple:
#Crypto Math #64: In 2017, Monero found a bug that could have let someone create unlimited coins undetected. It was patched quietly first; Monero's chain was never exploited.

A curve detail let the same coin be spent up to 8 times with different-looking tags. The extra coins would have been undetectable to outside observers.

card.title: Monero's quietly patched coin bug
card.sub: A torsion point trick could create coins undetected. The chain was never exploited.

long: Ethereum's consensus layer does not use secp256k1. Validators sign with BLS on the BLS12-381 curve: public keys are 48-byte compressed G1 points and signatures 96-byte compressed G2 points, verified with pairings. BLS signatures can be aggregated.
tech:
#Crypto Math #65: Ethereum's consensus layer doesn't use secp256k1. Validators sign with BLS on the BLS12-381 curve: public keys are 48-byte compressed G1 points, signatures 96-byte compressed G2 points.

Verification uses pairings, and BLS signatures can be aggregated, which is why Ethereum chose them for validator votes.
simple:
#Crypto Math #65: Ethereum validators don't sign with secp256k1. They use BLS signatures on the BLS12-381 curve, which can be merged together.

Normal Ethereum accounts still use secp256k1, like Bitcoin. The special curve is only for validators, because there are so many votes to check every few seconds.

card.title: Ethereum validators sign differently
card.sub: They use BLS on the BLS12-381 curve, not secp256k1, and signatures can merge.

long: BLS signatures can be aggregated: signatures on the same message combine into one 96-byte signature, verified against the aggregate public key in one check. Ethereum uses this so many validators' votes become one signature; Altair's sync committee has 512 validators.
tech:
#Crypto Math #66: BLS aggregation: signatures on the same message combine into one 96-byte signature, verified against the aggregate public key in one check.

Ethereum uses this so many validators' votes become one signature; Altair's sync committee has 512 validators, whose votes fit in a single 96-byte signature.
simple:
#Crypto Math #66: BLS signatures add up: hundreds of Ethereum validators can sign, and the result is a single signature checked in one go.

Without that trick, nodes would have to store and check hundreds of thousands of separate signatures. Aggregation makes Ethereum's large validator set workable.

card.title: Hundreds of votes, one signature
card.sub: BLS signatures on one message combine into a single 96-byte signature.

long: EIP-2333 defines key derivation for BLS12-381 validator keys. Each child key is derived through intermediate Lamport keys. Lamport is a hash-based signature scheme, so these keys are meant as a post-quantum backup in case BLS12-381 is ever no longer considered secure.
tech:
#Crypto Math #67: EIP-2333 defines key derivation for BLS12-381 validator keys. Each child key is derived through intermediate Lamport keys.

Lamport is a hash-based signature scheme, so these keys are meant as a post-quantum backup in case BLS12-381 is ever no longer considered secure.
simple:
#Crypto Math #67: Ethereum validator keys hide a quantum plan B: their derivation goes through hash-based Lamport keys, meant as a bridge if BLS ever breaks.

Hash-based schemes are believed to resist quantum computers. Building them into key derivation leaves a door open for a future migration.

card.title: A quantum plan B for validator keys
card.sub: EIP-2333 derives keys through hash-based Lamport keys, a post-quantum backup.

long: EIP-196 and EIP-197 added precompiled contracts for the alt_bn128 curve (also called BN254): point addition, scalar multiplication and pairing checks. They make the curve math used by zkSNARKs cheap enough that proofs can be verified within the block gas limit.
tech:
#Crypto Math #68: EIP-196 and EIP-197 added precompiled contracts for the alt_bn128 curve (BN254): point addition, scalar multiplication and pairing checks.

They make the curve math used by zkSNARKs cheap enough that proofs can be verified within the block gas limit. Most early on-chain ZK apps rely on them.
simple:
#Crypto Math #68: Ethereum has built-in shortcuts for the curve math used by zero-knowledge proofs. Without them, checking such a proof would cost too much gas.

Written in normal contract code, the math would be far too slow. As native functions, they made privacy apps and ZK rollups possible on Ethereum.

card.title: Built-in shortcuts for ZK proofs
card.sub: Precompiles for alt_bn128 make zkSNARK checks fit within the block gas limit.

long: Zcash's original (pre-Sapling) zk-SNARK system had a flaw that could have allowed undetectable counterfeiting. Ariel Gabizon found it on March 1, 2018. It was fixed by the Sapling upgrade on Oct 28, 2018 and disclosed on Feb 5, 2019, with no evidence of exploitation.
tech:
#Crypto Math #69: Zcash's original (pre-Sapling) zk-SNARK system had a flaw that could have allowed undetectable counterfeiting. Ariel Gabizon found it on Mar 1, 2018.

It was fixed by the Sapling upgrade on Oct 28, 2018 and disclosed on Feb 5, 2019, with no evidence of exploitation.
simple:
#Crypto Math #69: In 2018, a Zcash engineer found a flaw in its zero-knowledge proof system that could have allowed invisible counterfeiting. Fixed in Oct 2018, made public in Feb 2019.

The team stayed quiet until the fix was live, so nobody could exploit it in the meantime. No sign that anyone ever did.

card.title: A counterfeiting flaw in Zcash's proofs
card.sub: Found in March 2018, fixed by Sapling that October, no evidence of exploitation.

long: Ethereum's KZG ceremony ran from Jan 13 to Aug 8, 2023, 208 days, and collected 141,416 contributions to the setup used by EIP-4844 blob commitments. Its trust model is 1-of-N: it is secure as long as at least one contributor was honest and destroyed their secret.
tech:
#Crypto Math #70: Ethereum's KZG ceremony ran from Jan 13 to Aug 8, 2023 (208 days) and collected 141,416 contributions to the setup used by EIP-4844 blob commitments.

Its trust model is 1-of-N: secure as long as at least one contributor was honest and destroyed their secret.
simple:
#Crypto Math #70: Ethereum's 2023 setup ceremony collected 141,416 contributions. It stays secure as long as just one participant was honest and destroyed their secret.

Anyone could join from a browser. With so many people, the odds that all of them cheated together are tiny. That's the point.

card.title: Secure if just one person was honest
card.sub: Ethereum's KZG ceremony ran 208 days in 2023 for EIP-4844 blob commitments.

long: An EIP-4844 blob is 4096 BLS12-381 field elements of 32 bytes each, 128 KiB of data for layer-2 networks. Each blob gets a KZG commitment, and transactions reference it by a versioned hash: 0x01 followed by SHA256(commitment) without its first byte. Nodes can check the data against the commitment.
tech:
#Crypto Math #71: An EIP-4844 blob is 4096 BLS12-381 field elements of 32 bytes each: 128 KiB of data for layer-2 networks. Each blob gets a KZG commitment.

Txs reference it by a versioned hash: 0x01 || SHA256(commitment) without its first byte. Nodes can check the data against the commitment.
simple:
#Crypto Math #71: Ethereum "blobs" carry data for layer-2 networks. Each blob gets a short cryptographic commitment, so nodes can check the data without trusting anyone.

A blob holds 128 KiB. Instead of keeping it forever like normal data, nodes keep it for a limited time, which makes it much cheaper for layer-2s.

card.title: What an Ethereum blob holds
card.sub: 4096 field elements of 32 bytes, each blob checked against a KZG commitment.

long: The quantum threat: per BIP360, Shor's algorithm lets a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) solve the discrete log problem exponentially faster than classical methods, so it could derive ECDSA or Schnorr private keys from public keys. BIP360 says it is unclear when or if CRQCs will become viable.
tech:
#Crypto Math #72: The quantum threat, per BIP360: Shor's algorithm lets a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) solve the discrete log problem exponentially faster than classical methods.

It could derive ECDSA or Schnorr private keys from public keys. BIP360 says it's unclear when or if CRQCs will become viable.
simple:
#Crypto Math #72: The quantum threat in short: Shor's algorithm, on a large enough quantum computer, could derive a private key from a public key. Nobody knows when or if such a machine will exist.

Today's quantum computers are far too small. But since upgrades take years, Bitcoin developers are already discussing how to prepare.

card.title: The quantum threat in one algorithm
card.sub: Shor's algorithm could derive private keys from public keys. No one knows when or if.

long: BIP360 separates quantum attacks by exposure. Long exposure attacks target public keys already visible on-chain: P2PK outputs (e.g. Satoshi's coins), reused addresses and Taproot outputs, which could be attacked at leisure. Short exposure attacks must recover a key while a transaction waits in the mempool, before confirmation, which needs faster machines.
tech:
#Crypto Math #73: BIP360 separates quantum attacks by exposure. Long exposure: public keys already visible on-chain, like P2PK outputs (e.g. Satoshi's coins), reused addresses and Taproot outputs, attackable at leisure.

Short exposure: recover a key while a tx waits in the mempool, before confirmation, which needs much faster machines.
simple:
#Crypto Math #73: Not all coins face the same quantum risk. Coins whose public key is already on-chain, like Satoshi-era coins, could be attacked at leisure.

Coins at a never-used, hashed address only reveal their key when spent. An attacker would then have to crack it in minutes, before the payment confirms.

card.title: Not all coins face the same quantum risk
card.sub: Coins with public keys already on-chain, like Satoshi's, could be attacked at leisure.

long: On Aug 13, 2024, NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum standards: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from Kyber) for key encapsulation, and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from Dilithium) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+), both signature schemes. Quantum-safe signatures therefore already exist as standards.
tech:
#Crypto Math #74: Aug 13, 2024: NIST released its first three finalized post-quantum standards: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, from Kyber) for key encapsulation, FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, from Dilithium) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, from SPHINCS+), both signature schemes.

Quantum-safe signatures already exist as standards; the challenge is fitting them into blockchains.
simple:
#Crypto Math #74: Quantum-safe signatures already exist on paper. NIST published its first post-quantum standards in August 2024, two of them for digital signatures.

The catch for blockchains: these signatures are much bigger than today's 64-byte ones. Fitting them in without blowing up fees is the hard part.

card.title: Quantum-safe signatures already exist
card.sub: NIST finalized its first post-quantum standards in August 2024, two for signatures.

long: BIP360, still Draft, proposes Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), renamed in Feb 2026 from P2TSH (earlier P2QRH): outputs like Taproot but with the key-path spend removed, so no public key sits exposed in the output. This resists long exposure quantum attacks; protection against short exposure attacks may need post-quantum signatures.
tech:
#Crypto Math #75: BIP360 (Draft) proposes Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), renamed in Feb 2026 from P2TSH (earlier P2QRH): outputs like Taproot but with the key-path spend removed, so no public key sits exposed in the output.

This resists long exposure quantum attacks; protection against short exposure may need post-quantum signatures.
simple:
#Crypto Math #75: One Bitcoin quantum proposal, BIP360 (P2MR), is Taproot without the public-key shortcut, so keys aren't left exposed on-chain. It's still a draft.

It protects coins sitting in wallets for years. Protecting the moment of spending would need new, quantum-safe signatures on top.

card.title: Taproot without the key path
card.sub: The P2MR draft leaves no public key exposed, resisting long exposure attacks.

long: Recap: coins rest on a random private key, the secp256k1 curve and its ECDLP (128-bit security), hash functions like SHA-256 and Keccak, ECDSA then Schnorr signatures, BLS aggregation, BIP39/BIP32 seeds and ZK proofs. The math holds up; most real losses came from nonce reuse, weak randomness and sloppy code.
tech:
#Crypto Math #76: Recap: coins rest on a random private key, secp256k1 and its ECDLP (128-bit security), SHA-256 and Keccak, ECDSA then Schnorr, BLS aggregation, BIP39/32 seeds and ZK proofs.

The math holds up; most real losses came from nonce reuse, weak randomness and sloppy code. Follow for more.
simple:
#Crypto Math #76: Recap: your coins rest on a random number, one curve, a few hash functions and signatures. The math holds up; losses come from bad randomness and sloppy code.

Sony, Android wallets, Milk Sad, Profanity: the biggest failures in this series came from implementation mistakes, not from the core math being broken. Follow for more series.

card.title: The math holds, the code fails
card.sub: Most real losses came from nonce reuse, weak randomness and sloppy code.
